what_its_for: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant used to treat depression. It helps improve your mood, sleep, appetite, and energy levels. Your doctor may also prescribe it for other conditions not listed here.
how_to_take: Take mirtazapine by mouth, with or without food. If you are using the dissolving tablet (SolTab), place it on your tongue and let it dissolve completely — do not chew or swallow it whole. Do not split the dissolving tablet. Take it at the same time each day, usually at bedtime because it can make you sleepy. Do not stop taking mirtazapine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 15 mg once daily at bedtime. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose up to 45 mg per day depending on how you respond and how well you tolerate the medication. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store mirtazapine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the dissolving tablets in their original foil packaging until you are ready to use them. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking mirtazapine — it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and may be dangerous. Do not drive a car or operate heavy machinery until you know how this medication affects you, especially in the first few weeks. Avoid taking other medications that cause drowsiness without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first. Do not take mirtazapine within 14 days of taking an MAO inhibitor (such as phenelzine, selegiline, or linezolid) as this combination can cause a serious, life-threatening reaction.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of hurting yourself or suicide (especially in children, teens, or young adults — risk may be higher in the first few weeks), severe allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing), very high fever, stiff muscles, confusion, or fast heartbeat (signs of serotonin syndrome), unusual bleeding or bruising, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), seizures, very low sodium levels (signs include headache, confusion, weakness), or severe dizziness or fainting. Also contact your doctor if you feel more depressed, anxious, restless, or have new or worsening mood or behavior changes.
when_it_works: Mirtazapine may start improving your sleep and appetite within the first 1 to 2 weeks. However, it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks of regular use to feel the full antidepressant benefit. Be patient and keep taking it as directed even if you do not feel better right away. Talk to your doctor if you do not notice any improvement after several weeks.
special_populations: Older adults: Mirtazapine can cause more dizziness and drowsiness in older people, which increases the risk of falls. Use with caution and start at lower doses. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using mirtazapine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It may pass into breast milk. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease, as the medication may stay in your body longer. Children and teenagers: This medication is not FDA-approved for use in people under 18 years old. Young people may have a higher risk of suicidal thoughts when starting an antidepressant — monitor closely and contact your doctor immediately if this occurs.
